subject: ela
intro: Each passage below is a complete short informational text. The author's purpose or point of view is conveyed through tone, loaded word choice, the details that are emphasized or left out, and the way opposing views are handled. Read closely and explain how several of the author's choices work together. Do not give your own opinion. Stay with what the author's language reveals.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

Every few months a new gadget promises to fix the way children learn. The latest is a tablet program that drills math facts with cartoon mascots and flashing rewards. Supporters point out that scores on timed quizzes climbed in the first weeks. That much is true. But a timed quiz is not the same as understanding, and a flashing reward is not the same as curiosity. Watch a child after the novelty fades and you will see thumbs tapping faster while eyes glaze over. Companies that sell these programs rarely mention the studies showing that gains vanish within a year once the prizes stop. They prefer to show you the happy first week. Real learning is slow, sometimes boring, and built by a patient teacher who notices when a single student is lost. No mascot can do that. Before a district spends its budget on the newest blinking promise, it should ask a harder question than whether scores went up for a month. It should ask whether anything was actually learned.

Explain how the author's word choice and handling of the supporters' argument work together to convey the author's point of view about the math program. Use at least two specific words or phrases from the passage.
items.answer: The author is critical of the math program and doubts it produces real learning. This is shown by loaded phrases such as 'blinking promise,' 'flashing rewards,' and 'eyes glaze over,' which carry a dismissive, negative feeling, and by the way the author admits the supporters' point ('That much is true') only to undercut it immediately by arguing that higher quiz scores are 'not the same as understanding.' Granting the opposing point just to dismiss it reveals that the author firmly opposes the program.

steps: Determine the topic and the task: the topic is a tablet math program; the task is to explain how word choice and the handling of the supporters' argument reveal the author's stance.
Find the author's stance: the author distrusts the program and thinks it does not create real learning.
Collect loaded language: 'blinking promise,' 'flashing rewards,' 'eyes glaze over,' and 'thumbs tapping faster' all carry negative, mechanical, joyless feelings.

Analyze the counterargument: the author concedes the supporters' point ('That much is true') only to immediately argue that quiz scores are 'not the same as understanding,' which is a concede-then-dismiss move.
Combine the two: the negative words plus the dismissal of the opposing view work together to show a clearly critical, not neutral, point of view.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

Some people want to ban students from bringing phones to school entirely. Their worry is understandable. A buzzing pocket can pull a mind off a lesson, and no one learns algebra while scrolling videos. But a total ban treats every student like a problem to be managed rather than a person to be trusted. Phones are also calculators, dictionaries, cameras for science projects, and lifelines to a parent in an emergency. A locked-away phone cannot text a worried mom that practice ran late. The better path is not banning but teaching: clear rules about when phones stay in the bag, and lessons in using them well. Schools already teach students to handle scissors, chemicals, and the internet responsibly instead of forbidding all three. A phone deserves the same respect. We do not build judgment by removing every chance to practice it. We build it by guiding students through the very choices they will face for the rest of their lives.

The author raises the opposing view that phones distract students. Explain how the author treats that opposing view and what that treatment reveals about the author's own point of view.
items.answer: The author treats the opposing view with respect but does not accept it, calling the worry 'understandable' and even agreeing that 'no one learns algebra while scrolling videos.' The author then sets it aside by arguing that a total ban 'treats every student like a problem' and by listing the useful things phones do, like serving as a lifeline in an emergency. By acknowledging the concern only to argue past it, the author reveals a point of view that opposes banning phones and instead favors teaching students to use them responsibly.

steps: Identify the opposing view the author names: that phones distract students from learning.
Notice how the author treats it: politely, calling the worry 'understandable' and conceding 'no one learns algebra while scrolling videos.'
See the pivot: the word 'But' signals the author is acknowledging the view only to argue against it.
Identify the author's actual stance: against a total ban and in favor of teaching responsible use, shown by the comparison to scissors, chemicals, and the internet.
Connect the treatment to the stance: granting the opposing point respectfully and then overriding it shows the author disagrees with the ban while still sounding fair.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

The city council calls its new downtown plan a bold step forward. Look closely at what the step actually involves. Three blocks of small, family-owned shops, some open for forty years, would be cleared to make room for a parking structure and a chain coffee outlet. The plan's supporters speak of progress and modern convenience. They speak less about the tailor, the bakery, and the hardware store that will simply disappear. A neighborhood is not a blank lot waiting to be improved. It is a web of people who know one another's names. You can pour concrete over that web, but you cannot pour it back. The council promises that new businesses will bring jobs. Perhaps. But a job pouring chain coffee is not the same as a livelihood built over a lifetime, and a parking garage is not a community. Before the bulldozers arrive, the people who actually live here deserve to be asked what they would lose.

The council describes the plan as progress. Explain how the author uses word choice and the selection of details to convey a point of view that differs from the council's. Cite at least two specific details or phrases.
items.answer: The author opposes the plan and sees it as a loss rather than progress. The author chooses details that highlight what disappears, naming 'the tailor, the bakery, and the hardware store' and shops 'open for forty years,' while reducing the replacements to a 'parking structure' and a 'chain coffee outlet.' Loaded phrases like 'pour concrete over that web' and 'a parking garage is not a community' carry a sad, disapproving feeling. By emphasizing the human cost and downplaying the council's promise of jobs with the doubtful word 'Perhaps,' the author conveys a point of view that the plan destroys something valuable, contradicting the council's claim of progress.

steps: Note the contrast set up in the passage: the council says 'progress,' but the author signals doubt with 'Look closely at what the step actually involves.'
Identify emphasized details: specific beloved shops (tailor, bakery, hardware store), forty years of history, the human 'web' of a neighborhood.
Identify the diminished details: the replacements are flattened to a 'parking structure' and 'chain coffee outlet,' and the jobs promise gets only a skeptical 'Perhaps.'
Spot loaded language: 'pour concrete over that web,' 'you cannot pour it back,' and 'a parking garage is not a community' all carry disapproval.
Combine: detail selection plus loaded language work together to convey a critical stance opposed to the council's framing of progress.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

Volcanoes form where the Earth's heat finds a path to the surface. Deep underground, rock melts into magma. When pressure builds, the magma rises through cracks in the crust. Some volcanoes erupt with slow rivers of lava that creep downhill, while others explode with ash and gas that shoot miles into the sky. Scientists classify volcanoes by their shape and the kind of material they release. Shield volcanoes, like those in Hawaii, are broad and gently sloped because their lava flows easily. Stratovolcanoes, such as Mount Fuji, are steep and cone-shaped because thicker lava and ash pile up near the vent. Monitoring stations measure small earthquakes and swelling ground to warn nearby towns when an eruption may be near. Studying volcanoes helps people understand both the dangers they pose and the rich soil they leave behind.

A student says the author's point of view is that volcanoes are dangerous and frightening. Explain why that is an inaccurate reading, and state the author's actual purpose, using evidence from the passage.
items.answer: That reading is inaccurate because the author does not use frightened or alarmed language and treats both the dangers and the benefits evenly, ending by noting volcanoes leave 'rich soil.' The passage explains how volcanoes form, classifies them by type with neutral examples like Hawaii and Mount Fuji, and describes how monitoring works. The author's actual purpose is to inform and explain how volcanoes form and how they are studied, not to persuade the reader to feel fear. The student mistook the topic, which involves danger, for the author's attitude, which is neutral and explanatory.

steps: Check for loaded or emotional language: there is none; words are descriptive and factual, such as 'classify,' 'measure,' and 'monitoring stations.'
Check how dangers are handled: danger is mentioned but balanced against benefits ('rich soil they leave behind'), showing no one-sided alarm.
Identify the structure: a definition, a process, a classification with examples, and a note on monitoring, all hallmarks of an informational, explanatory text.
State the actual purpose: to inform and explain how volcanoes form and are studied.
Name the misreading: the student confused the topic (which involves danger) with the author's attitude (neutral), assuming the subject equals the stance.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

There is a quiet argument over whether middle schoolers should be assigned summer reading. On one side, teachers note that skills slip over a long break and that a single required book keeps minds awake. On the other, families point out that summer is short and childhood shorter, and that a forced book can sour a young reader on reading altogether. Both sides have a point worth hearing. A child who reads nothing for ten weeks does return rusty. Yet a child made to slog through a book chosen by someone else may learn only that reading is a chore. Perhaps the honest answer is that it depends on the book and the child. A thin, exciting novel offered with real choice is one thing; a thick, dull assignment with a test attached is another. The research itself is mixed, with studies pointing in both directions. What seems clear is that the goal should be a reader who wants to keep reading, and any policy that forgets that goal has missed the point.

Explain how the author's handling of both sides reveals the author's purpose, and explain why it would be wrong to call the author simply 'against summer reading.'
items.answer: The author presents both sides fairly, granting that skills 'slip over a long break' and that a forced book can 'sour a young reader,' and even says 'Both sides have a point worth hearing.' The author also admits 'The research itself is mixed.' This balanced handling shows the author's purpose is to weigh a debate thoughtfully and arrive at a nuanced position, not to argue one side. It would be wrong to call the author 'against summer reading' because the author allows that the right book with real choice can work; the author's actual position is that it depends on the book and the child and that the goal is keeping kids reading.

steps: Identify both viewpoints: pro summer reading (skills slip) and against (forced reading sours readers).
Notice the even handling: the author concedes a real point to each side and says 'Both sides have a point worth hearing' and 'The research itself is mixed.'
Determine the purpose: to weigh the debate carefully and reach a thoughtful, conditional conclusion, not to persuade for one fixed side.
Find the author's actual position: 'it depends on the book and the child,' favoring real choice and exciting books.
Explain the misreading: calling the author simply 'against' ignores the concessions and the conditional stance, confusing a balanced, nuanced view with one-sided opposition.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

The new sports drink in the school vending machines arrives wrapped in the language of health. The label boasts electrolytes, energy, and a splash of vitamin C, as if a workout in a bottle. Read past the bright colors and the picture is less impressive. A single bottle holds nearly as much sugar as a candy bar, a fact printed in small gray type on the back. The electrolytes amount to a pinch of salt that any meal already supplies. As for the energy, that is simply the sugar again, wearing a friendlier name. Companies are skilled at dressing sweetened water in athletic clothing, because an image of a sprinting athlete sells better than a spoonful of sugar. None of this is illegal, and the drink will not harm a student who has one now and then. But families and schools deserve to see the product plainly, not through the haze of a clever advertisement.

Explain how the author's word choice and the contrast the author builds work together to convey the author's point of view about the sports drink. Cite at least two specific phrases.
items.answer: The author is skeptical of the sports drink and sees its health claims as marketing tricks. The author builds a contrast between the bright 'language of health' on the front and the 'small gray type on the back,' between the promised 'energy' and the truth that it is 'simply the sugar again, wearing a friendlier name.' Loaded phrases like 'sweetened water in athletic clothing' and reading 'past the bright colors' carry a distrustful, exposing tone. The contrast between the flashy image and the plain facts works with this word choice to convey a point of view that the drink is dressed-up sugar, not real health.

steps: Identify the structure: the author sets the drink's image against its reality.
List image words: 'language of health,' 'boasts electrolytes,' 'bright colors,' 'athletic clothing.'
List reality words: 'nearly as much sugar as a candy bar,' 'small gray type on the back,' 'simply the sugar again, wearing a friendlier name.'
Note the tone: phrases like 'sweetened water in athletic clothing' reveal distrust and an intent to expose.
Combine: the deliberate image-versus-reality contrast plus the skeptical word choice convey a critical point of view toward the marketing.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

Supporters of starting the school day later make a fair-sounding case. Teenagers, they note, are wired to fall asleep late and wake late, so a 7:30 bell forces them to learn while half asleep. There is truth here, and anyone who has watched a sleepy ninth grader stare blankly at a whiteboard understands it. Yet the supporters rarely follow the schedule to its end. Push the start time back an hour and the final bell rings an hour later too. After-school jobs, sports practice, and the younger siblings a teen must walk home all collide with that later finish. Buses that now carry elementary and high school students in two trips may need a second fleet the district cannot afford. None of this means teenagers do not need sleep. It means a real solution must weigh the whole day, not just the morning. A plan that fixes the sunrise and breaks the sunset has not solved the problem. It has only moved it.

The author agrees that teenagers need sleep. Explain how the author can grant that point and still hold a point of view that opposes the later start time. Use evidence from the passage.
items.answer: The author grants the sleep point ('There is truth here') but still opposes the later start time by arguing that supporters 'rarely follow the schedule to its end.' The author shifts attention to the consequences of a later finish, naming after-school jobs, sports practice, walking younger siblings home, and the cost of a second bus fleet. By conceding the morning problem while emphasizing the new problems a later finish creates, the author reveals a point of view that the later start is not a real solution. The closing line, that the plan 'has only moved' the problem, makes the opposing stance clear even though the author respects the supporters' concern.

steps: Identify the concession: 'There is truth here,' acknowledging teens need sleep.
Spot the pivot word 'Yet,' which signals the author is about to argue against the supporters.
List the author's emphasized costs: later finish, after-school jobs, sports, walking siblings home, an unaffordable second bus fleet.
Read the closing judgment: the plan 'has only moved' the problem, not solved it.
Explain the combination: conceding one point while stacking up the downsides of the proposed fix is how the author stays opposed without sounding unreasonable.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

The town's plan to install bright streetlights along the river trail sounds, at first, like simple safety. Who could argue against being able to see? But step onto that trail after dark today and you find a different kind of value. Fireflies blink over the water. Owls hunt in the hush. Stargazers lie on the grass and watch a sky most city children never see. Floodlights would erase all of it in a single switch. Studies show that bright artificial light at night confuses migrating birds, drives away insects that fish and bats depend on, and disrupts the sleep of people in nearby homes. Safety matters, no one denies it, and a few low, shielded lamps at the trailheads would help walkers find their way. But drowning a living darkness in white glare is not safety. It is the loss of something rare, traded for a feeling of security that gentler lighting could provide just as well.

Explain how the author's word choice and the details the author chooses to include reveal a point of view that differs from the plan's framing of 'simple safety.' Cite at least two specific words or details.
items.answer: The author opposes the bright floodlights and values the dark trail as it is. The author selects vivid details of what the dark offers, 'Fireflies blink over the water,' 'Owls hunt in the hush,' and stargazers watching the sky, while describing the lights as something that would 'erase all of it in a single switch' and 'drowning a living darkness in white glare.' These loaded phrases carry loss and disapproval. By admitting safety matters but offering gentler lamps instead, the author reveals a point of view that the bright plan destroys something rare, which differs sharply from the plan's framing of 'simple safety.'

steps: Note the plan's framing the author quotes: 'simple safety,' and the author's challenge: 'step onto that trail after dark today and you find a different kind of value.'
Identify the celebrated details: fireflies, owls, stargazers, migrating birds, fish, and bats, all things the dark protects.
Identify the loaded language for the lights: 'erase all of it in a single switch' and 'drowning a living darkness in white glare.'
See the concession-and-alternative: the author admits safety matters but proposes 'low, shielded lamps' instead of floodlights.
Combine: the emphasized natural details plus the negative imagery for the lights convey a stance that opposes the bright plan, contrary to the 'simple safety' framing.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

The printing press changed the world more than almost any machine before it. Before its arrival in the fifteenth century, books were copied by hand, a slow labor that could take a scribe months for a single volume. Such books were rare and costly, owned mostly by the wealthy and by monasteries. When Johannes Gutenberg arranged movable metal letters and pressed inked type onto paper, a book that once took months could be produced in days, and then in hours. Prices fell. Ideas that once crept from town to town now traveled in printed sheets. More people learned to read because more had something to read. Scholars could compare exact copies rather than error-filled handwritten ones. The press did not invent knowledge, but it spread knowledge widely for the first time, and the spread of knowledge reshaped religion, science, and government across Europe.

A student claims the author's point of view is that the printing press was harmful because it caused conflict in religion and government. Explain why this is a misreading, and state the author's actual purpose, citing evidence.
items.answer: This is a misreading because the author never calls the press harmful and uses no negative or warning language. The author writes admiringly, saying the press 'changed the world more than almost any machine before it' and 'spread knowledge widely for the first time.' The mention of religion, science, and government describes the press's wide influence, not damage. The author's actual purpose is to inform and explain how the printing press worked and why it mattered historically. The student overstated and twisted a neutral, even positive, description into a warning the text does not support.

steps: Scan for negative or warning words: there are none; instead the author uses 'changed the world,' 'spread knowledge widely,' and 'reshaped.'
Re-read the line about religion, science, and government: it lists areas the press influenced, framed as significance, not harm.
Determine the author's tone: admiring and explanatory toward the invention.
State the actual purpose: to inform and explain the history and importance of the printing press.
Name the error: the student overstated and reversed the author's stance, reading harm into a passage that presents the press positively.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

The brochure for the new amusement park promises the thrill of a lifetime, and it is easy to be swept along. Towering coasters, it says, in a setting of natural beauty. What the glossy pages do not mention is the forest that stood there last spring. Three hundred acres of old woodland, home to deer, foxes, and a creek where children once caught crayfish, were cleared so that the towers could rise. The brochure shows a single small tree planted near the entrance, as if that settles the account. It calls the park eco-friendly because the roller coasters run partly on solar power. A solar-powered ride on a flattened forest is still a flattened forest. There is nothing wrong with loving a good coaster. But a company that bulldozes the woods and then sells the result as a celebration of nature is selling more than tickets. It is selling a story that does not match the ground beneath it.

Explain how the author uses the contrast between the brochure's claims and the omitted details to convey a point of view. Cite at least two specific details.
items.answer: The author distrusts the park and sees its nature claims as dishonest. The author contrasts the brochure's promises, a 'setting of natural beauty' and the label 'eco-friendly,' with the details the brochure leaves out, the 'three hundred acres of old woodland' and the deer, foxes, and crayfish creek that were 'cleared.' The pointed lines 'A solar-powered ride on a flattened forest is still a flattened forest' and 'a story that does not match the ground beneath it' reveal a critical, exposing tone. By emphasizing the omitted destruction against the brochure's cheerful claims, the author conveys a point of view that the park's nature image is false advertising.

steps: Identify the brochure's claims the author quotes: 'thrill of a lifetime,' 'natural beauty,' 'eco-friendly.'
Identify the omitted details the author supplies: 300 acres of old woodland, deer, foxes, a crayfish creek, all cleared.
Note the single token tree 'as if that settles the account,' which the author uses to mock the eco claim.
Spot the loaded judgments: 'a flattened forest is still a flattened forest' and 'a story that does not match the ground beneath it.'
Combine: the contrast between cheerful claims and hidden destruction conveys a critical point of view that the park's green image is misleading.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

Should cities replace some bus routes with on-demand vans that riders summon by app? Two writers disagree. The first calls fixed bus routes 'a relic' and praises the vans as 'freedom on wheels,' picturing a rider whisked door to door without a wait. The second calls the vans 'a toy for people with smartphones' and warns that riders without phones, or without steady internet, would be 'left standing at a corner that no longer has a bus.' Both writers agree the goal is getting people where they need to go. Both agree current buses can run late. Where they split is on who gets served. The first writer trusts that technology will reach everyone in time. The second points to elderly riders and low-income neighborhoods where it may not. Notice that the first writer never mentions those riders at all. What a writer leaves out can reveal as much as what a writer says.

The passage presents two writers. Explain what the first writer's point of view is, and explain how the detail the first writer leaves out helps reveal it. Use evidence from the passage.
items.answer: The first writer's point of view is strongly in favor of replacing buses with on-demand vans, shown by calling fixed routes 'a relic' and the vans 'freedom on wheels.' What the first writer leaves out helps reveal this stance: the passage points out that the first writer 'never mentions' riders without phones or internet, the elderly, or low-income neighborhoods. Leaving out the people who might be harmed shows the first writer is focused on the technology's promise and is optimistic, even one-sided, about it. As the passage says, what a writer leaves out can reveal as much as what a writer says.

steps: Separate the two writers: the first favors the vans, the second warns against them.
Identify the first writer's loaded language: 'a relic' for buses, 'freedom on wheels' for vans, signaling strong approval.
Find what the first writer omits: any mention of riders without phones, internet, the elderly, or low-income neighborhoods.
Connect the omission to stance: leaving out the people who could be hurt shows an optimistic, one-sided point of view favoring the technology.
Use the passage's own cue: 'What a writer leaves out can reveal as much as what a writer says,' which confirms omission as evidence of point of view.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

The county wants to thank you for recycling, and you should feel good about the bottles you rinse and sort. But the cheerful curbside bin tells only part of the story. Much of what we place there is never actually recycled. Certain plastics have no buyer, so they are quietly shipped overseas or buried in a landfill after all, while the homeowner imagines them reborn as park benches. Recycling is real and worthwhile for glass, metal, and paper, which genuinely return as new goods. For many plastics, though, the truth is grimmer. The most honest thing a person can do is not simply recycle more but buy less of the throwaway plastic in the first place. A bottle never made is a bottle that never needs sorting, shipping, or burying. The county's program is not a lie. It is just an incomplete story, and the part left untold is the part that matters most.

Explain how the author's purpose goes beyond simply praising recycling, and how word choice such as 'quietly,' 'grimmer,' and 'incomplete story' helps convey the author's point of view. Cite the passage.
items.answer: The author's purpose goes beyond praising recycling: the author wants to expose that much plastic 'is never actually recycled' and to persuade readers to buy less throwaway plastic. The word 'quietly' suggests something is being hidden when plastics are 'quietly shipped overseas.' The word 'grimmer' frames the plastic truth as bad news. Calling the program 'an incomplete story' with 'the part left untold' being 'the part that matters most' reveals a point of view that the cheerful recycling image is misleading. Together these choices convey a critical stance toward how recycling is presented and a push toward reducing plastic, not just sorting it.

steps: Identify the surface message: the county thanks you for recycling.
Find the deeper purpose: to reveal that many plastics are not recycled and to urge buying less, shown by 'buy less of the throwaway plastic in the first place.'
Analyze 'quietly': it implies concealment in 'quietly shipped overseas.'
Analyze 'grimmer': it casts the plastic reality as troubling.

Analyze 'incomplete story' and 'the part left untold is the part that matters most': these reveal a critical stance that the cheerful image hides the truth, so the purpose is persuasive, not merely celebratory.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

Honey bees are dying off in alarming numbers, and the writer wants you to know it is not too late. The piece opens with a question: what would breakfast look like without bees? No almonds, no blueberries, no apples, the writer answers, since bees pollinate a third of the food we eat. Then comes a list of small, doable actions: plant native flowers, skip the lawn chemicals, leave a shallow dish of water in the garden. The writer admits the problem is bigger than any backyard and that farms and lawmakers must act too. Still, the closing line urges the reader directly: 'Start with one pot of flowers on your own windowsill, and start this weekend.' The whole piece is built to move you from worry to action, opening with a vivid fear and ending with a task you can begin in days.

Explain how the author's opening question and closing call to action work together to convey the author's purpose. Use evidence from the passage.
items.answer: The author's purpose is to persuade readers to take action to help bees. The opening question, 'what would breakfast look like without bees,' followed by 'No almonds, no blueberries, no apples,' creates worry by making the loss feel personal. The closing line then directs the reader to act: 'Start with one pot of flowers on your own windowsill, and start this weekend.' These two choices work together by first raising a vivid fear and then handing the reader an easy first step, moving the reader 'from worry to action.' This opening-to-closing structure reveals a persuasive purpose, a call to act, not just an informative one.

steps: Identify the opening device: a question and the alarming answer about breakfast without bees, which creates concern.
Identify the closing device: a direct command to plant flowers and start this weekend.
Note the middle: a list of doable actions, which assumes the reader will do something.
Connect the structure: fear at the start plus a concrete task at the end is designed to move the reader to act.
State the purpose: to persuade and call the reader to action, as the passage itself says, 'built to move you from worry to action.'

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

Both coaches were asked the same question: should young athletes specialize in one sport year-round? Coach Ramirez answered carefully. 'Specializing early can build skill fast,' she said, 'but it also wears down growing bodies and burns out kids who never get a break.' She mentioned studies on overuse injuries and studies on athletes who thrived after focusing young, and she did not pretend either set of studies was the whole truth. Coach Bell answered differently. 'If you want to win,' he said, 'you commit to one sport and nothing else, period. Kids who play three sports are just average at all three.' Notice the difference in how each coach treats the other side. Ramirez weighs it. Bell waves it away. A reader can disagree with either coach, but the way each one handles the opposing view tells you how settled each one's mind already is.

Compare how the two coaches handle the opposing view, and explain what that handling reveals about each coach's point of view. Use evidence from the passage.
items.answer: Coach Ramirez handles the opposing view by weighing it: she admits specializing 'can build skill fast' but also 'wears down growing bodies,' and she cites studies on both sides without pretending either is 'the whole truth.' This balanced handling reveals an open, undecided point of view. Coach Bell handles the opposing view by waving it away, saying flatly 'you commit to one sport and nothing else, period,' and dismissing multi-sport kids as 'just average at all three.' His refusal to consider the other side reveals a firm, one-sided point of view in favor of early specialization. As the passage notes, the way each handles the opposing view shows 'how settled each one's mind already is.'

steps: Identify each coach's treatment of the other side: Ramirez weighs it; Bell waves it away.
Quote Ramirez's balance: concedes early specializing 'can build skill fast' but also 'wears down growing bodies,' and refuses to call either study 'the whole truth.'
Quote Bell's dismissal: 'one sport and nothing else, period' and multi-sport kids are 'just average at all three.'
Link handling to stance: weighing the opposing view shows an open mind; dismissing it shows a fixed, one-sided stance.
Use the passage's cue: how each handles the opposing view tells 'how settled each one's mind already is.'

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

The new museum exhibit on ancient Egypt is, the city says, a triumph of education. In some ways it is. The hall is filled with real artifacts, careful labels, and a respectful tone toward the people who made them. Yet read the signs closely and a quieter choice appears. The exhibit lingers on golden masks, jeweled coffins, and the treasures of a single boy-king, while the farmers, weavers, and laborers who built that world earn a single small panel near the exit. Most ancient Egyptians never saw a golden mask. They grew grain, hauled stone, and raised children along the river. An exhibit that shows only the gold tells a true story, but a narrow one, the story of the few rather than the many. To call it the whole of ancient Egypt would be to mistake the crown for the country.

Explain how the author's word choice and the author's point about what the exhibit emphasizes and leaves out work together to convey the author's point of view. Cite at least two specific details.
items.answer: The author admires the exhibit's craft but criticizes what it emphasizes. The author grants it has 'real artifacts' and a 'respectful tone,' then turns with 'Yet' to argue it 'lingers on golden masks, jeweled coffins, and the treasures of a single boy-king' while ordinary people, the 'farmers, weavers, and laborers,' get only 'a single small panel near the exit.' Phrases like 'a true story, but a narrow one' and 'mistake the crown for the country' carry a critical judgment. By contrasting the emphasized treasures with the omitted majority, the author conveys a point of view that the exhibit, though well made, tells an incomplete, lopsided story of ancient Egypt.

steps: Identify the concession: the author admits the exhibit has real artifacts and a respectful tone, 'In some ways it is' a triumph.
Spot the pivot 'Yet,' which introduces the author's criticism.
Identify what is emphasized versus omitted: golden masks and a boy-king's treasures get the spotlight; farmers, weavers, and laborers get 'a single small panel near the exit.'
Analyze loaded phrases: 'a true story, but a narrow one' and 'mistake the crown for the country' deliver a critical judgment.
